lead.headline: World Court Finds Myanmar Responsible for Genocide Against the Rohingya
lead.deck: Nine of the 15 judges in The Hague backed the finding in a case brought by The Gambia; Myanmar must pay compensation and let displaced Rohingya come home safely.
body: A small West African country has won a case it brought on behalf of people far from its own borders. Ruling on 19 November in The Gambia v. Myanmar, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the UN’s highest court, held Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, a Muslim minority, in a 2017 military crackdown. The finding, for events in the north of Rakhine state, was carried by 9 judges against 6, who also ruled that Myanmar neither prevented nor punished it. Never before has a State been found responsible in this way under the Genocide Convention.

The judges also laid out the toll. In the court’s account, roughly 10,000 Rohingya died in the 2017 “clearance operations” and some 700,000 escaped into Bangladesh. Close to 400 villages, around 40% of all those in three townships of northern Rakhine, were partly or completely destroyed. Myanmar’s position is that its army was responding to raids on police posts by Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army fighters.

Those findings carry duties. Myanmar must pay compensation, let displaced Rohingya come home in safety and dignity and only by their own choice, reunite separated families, and tell the court within two years what it has done. Over 1.3 million Rohingya are still displaced, some 1.2 million in the Cox’s Bazar camps in Bangladesh.
The Gambia, which filed the case in November 2019, hailed “a historic day for international justice”; UN chief Antonio Guterres called the judgment a “powerful recognition” of the victims.

world.headline: Europe Answers the Shenzhen Summit With a History Lesson: No New Yalta
world.deck: Germany’s Merz recalled how Europe was carved up in 1945; Putin replied that Yalta was not necessarily bad, and invited Europe’s leaders to Moscow.
body: The leaders of the US, Russia and China met as a trio for the first time in Shenzhen on 19 November, and Europe heard an echo of 1945. Their four-point “Declaration toward Peace” dealt with UN reform, oil supplies, the International Criminal Court and nuclear risk, yet said nothing about Russia’s war in Ukraine. Even before the talks, Russian lawmaker Pyotr Tolstoy, head of his parliament’s foreign affairs committee, had floated the label “new Yalta”.

Why does that name sting? In February 1945, at Yalta in Crimea, Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin settled much of post-war Europe’s shape. The Soviets pledged free elections in lands freed from Nazi rule, but Washington and London accepted that neighbouring Eastern European governments should be “friendly” to Moscow, and a declaration on Poland gave Communists a place in its post-war government. Yalta also produced the UN Security Council’s five permanent, veto-holding seats. Critics later accused Roosevelt of “handing over” Eastern Europe to the Soviet Union.

Meeting Ukraine’s backers in Berlin that day, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said a Yalta format “will not bring peace”, adding: “At Yalta, Europe was divided up.” He handed out fragments of the Berlin Wall. The 36-nation Coalition of the Willing, led by the UK, France and Germany, promised Ukraine more money and military help, the UK alone 10 billion pounds.

Moscow reads the history differently. Putin said the 1945 conference was not necessarily bad, since victory over Nazism was formally sealed there, and that Yalta “just codified the realities”. He turned down Kyiv’s call for a ceasefire before winter but invited Europe’s leaders to Moscow; Merz proposed a neutral venue such as the Emirates. In Washington on 20 November, Trump said Putin “clearly expressed his desire” to see the war end by diplomatic means.

india.headline: A Bhopal Lab Gives India Its Own Killed-Virus Vaccine Against H5N1 in Chickens
india.deck: Developed over three years by ICAR-NIHSAD, it targets the strain behind most outbreaks on Indian farms and may cost Rs 1 to Rs 2 a dose.
body: Until this week, Indian poultry farms had no vaccine made for the H5N1 bird flu strain that keeps returning to them. On Friday 20 November Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan launched one at a programme in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh: India’s first indigenous H5N1 vaccine for chickens, developed in the same city by the ICAR-National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (NIHSAD). The launch had been planned for Delhi, but Chouhan moved it to Bhopal because the scientists there had done the work.

The vaccine targets the H5N1 virus of clade 2.3.2.1a, a lineage of highly pathogenic avian influenza and the main strain found on Indian poultry farms; according to Insights IAS, no specific commercial vaccine for it existed in India or abroad. It is an inactivated, or killed-virus, vaccine. It contains virus particles that have been chemically made harmless and cannot multiply, yet they still train the chicken’s immune system to fight the real virus. Because the particles cannot replicate, the vaccine carries no risk of causing the infection itself. It was built from Indian virus samples collected since the country first detected H5N1 in 2006, and is designed for both commercial and backyard flocks.

The research took three years under strict biosafety rules: team members followed long sanitisation routines before going home, and were not allowed to keep other animals as pets. ICAR Director General Dr ML Jat estimated the price at Rs 1 to Rs 2 per dose, said talks with potential manufacturers on commercial production were under way, and hopes India can one day export the vaccine.

A cheap dose matters because the disease is common and deadly for birds. Chouhan said India has recorded more than 500 outbreaks of H5N1 and H5N8 bird flu since 2006. The first, at Navapur in Maharashtra, killed about 10 lakh chickens; nine lakh died in 2021 and two lakh this year, he said. Highly pathogenic bird flu can kill almost 100% of infected birds. To contain infection, farms have often had to cull, or kill, entire flocks. The vaccine is meant to prevent this, and is expected to help more than 90 lakh poultry farmers.

The wider stakes are economic and medical. Chouhan put yearly losses from livestock and poultry diseases at about Rs 56,000 crore, announced a Rs 300 crore modern laboratory in Bhopal, and called the vaccine “an example of India’s self-reliance.” The World Health Organization describes H5N1 as a flu virus that infects birds and mammals, and humans only in rare instances; the vaccine’s stated aims include curbing its spread from birds to mammals and humans.

politics_and_civics.headline: Rajasthan’s Rural Councils Swing to Congress, Though the BJP Runs the State
politics_and_civics.deck: Congress won 3,701 block-level seats to the BJP’s 2,181, and the ruling party says it will review its shortcomings.
body: Rural India governs itself through three layers of elected councils, and Rajasthan has just counted the votes for two of them. The 73rd Constitutional Amendment, passed by Parliament in 1992 and in force from 24 April 1993, made panchayats “institutions of self government”. States with more than 25 lakh people have three tiers: the Gram Panchayat in the village, the Panchayat Samiti at block level and the Zila Parishad at district level. A State Election Commission in each state holds these elections every five years, and seats are reserved in proportion for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and women.

Counting for Panchayat Samiti and Zila Parishad seats took place on Friday 20 November in 37 of Rajasthan’s 41 districts, and the opposition came out ahead. By the evening, State Election Commission figures gave Congress 3,701 Panchayat Samiti seats and the BJP 2,181. In the Zila Parishads, Congress had 599 seats to the BJP’s 301. The count was not yet complete: results had been declared for 7,393 of 7,543 Panchayat Samiti seats and 981 of 1,275 Zila Parishad seats. The BSP and CPI(M) also won a few seats.

The lead was spread widely. Congress won more Panchayat Samiti seats than the BJP in 33 of the 37 districts, and led in 24 districts in the Zila Parishad polls to the BJP’s six. In Jaipur it took 216 Panchayat Samiti seats to the BJP’s 87. The BJP was ahead only in Ajmer, Balotra, Salumber and Udaipur; in Udaipur it won 146 seats to Congress’s 137. In Bharatpur, the Chief Minister’s home district, independents won 76 seats, ahead of Congress with 46 and the BJP with 32. Counting in Kota, Baran, Karauli and Sri Ganganagar was postponed to 17 December; the Daily Jagran links this to the current councils’ terms ending next month.

What makes the result notable is who runs the state. The BJP governs Rajasthan, and these results are the second major test for Chief Minister Bhajan Lal Sharma’s government. Former chief minister Ashok Gehlot of Congress called them a message from rural voters, farmers, workers and women against “government neglect and unfulfilled promises”. BJP spokesperson Ramlal Sharma said the party’s performance was “below expectations” and that it would review its shortcomings and work to improve.

economics.headline: Wall Street Slides Into a ‘Correction’ as AI Shares Lead a Week of Losses
economics.deck: By midday Friday the Standard & Poor’s 500 index was about 10% below its October record; Nvidia and newly listed Anthropic were among the hardest hit.
body: Stock markets have a name for a fall of this size. When an index closes more than 10% below its record, it is called a “correction”. On Friday 20 November the Standard & Poor’s 500 index fell about 2% by midday, leaving it about 10% below its 6 October record, and both it and the Dow Jones Industrial Average entered correction territory. The tech-heavy Nasdaq wiped out all its gains for 2026. The index was heading for a seventh straight daily loss, the longest streak since the COVID-19 pandemic began in 2020.

Artificial-intelligence companies led the slide. Anthropic’s share sale a day earlier was the largest ever: its shares rose about 17% on their first day, Thursday, then fell 12.4% to $85.16 on Friday, still above the $83 IPO price, the price at which the shares were first sold to the public. Chipmaker Nvidia dropped more than 12% after a Reuters report that the US Securities and Exchange Commission is examining possible accounting issues at the company.

Analysts pointed to several causes: doubts about AI spending, expectations of more US interest-rate rises to fight inflation, and leadership turmoil at Nvidia after Jensen Huang’s departure as chief executive. Charles Schwab’s Kevin Gordon described “dual forces” hitting the market: a hawkish Federal Reserve, meaning one inclined to raise rates, and the AI and tech slump. Over the whole week, CNBC’s Friday-afternoon tally had the Dow down about 7%, the Standard & Poor’s 500 almost 8% and the Nasdaq about 9%.

The selling spread well beyond New York. On Friday Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 5.06% and South Korea’s KOSPI 5.21%, while India’s Nifty 50 bucked the trend and rose 1.06%. The losses also reach ordinary families: NBC News noted the downturn is especially hard on households relying on 401(k) retirement accounts and pensions, which hold shares.

science_and_technology.headline: Voyager 1 Is Now One Light-Day From Earth, 49 Years After Its Launch
science_and_technology.deck: A command now needs a day to arrive and a day for the reply, and engineers are working out why the probe has sent no data since 14 November.
body: Space is so vast that distances there are often measured in time. NASA’s Voyager 1 is now one light-day from Earth: the probe passed that mark at 2:16 a.m. Pacific time (5:16 a.m. Eastern) on 18 November. A light-day is the distance light covers in a day, about 16.1 billion miles or 25.9 billion km, and light moves at about 186,000 miles (299,000 km) every second. Sunlight reaches the Moon in about 1.3 seconds and Neptune in about four hours; it needs roughly 20 more hours to get as far as Voyager 1, the most distant object people have ever built.

Talking to the probe is now a two-day job. NASA’s Deep Space Network, which uses large antennas at three sites around the world, needs 24 hours to get a command out to Voyager 1, and the answer takes another 24 hours to come back. The team at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in California heard from the probe 24 hours later. “We listen to Voyager 1 every day,” said NASA’s Suzanne Dodd, “and send commands to the spacecraft weekly.”

There is a problem, though. No science or engineering data have arrived from Voyager 1 since 14 November. The probe still sends its carrier signal, the radio wave that normally carries those data, and engineers used it together with calculations of the spacecraft’s path to confirm the milestone while they work out what has gone wrong. Ageing hardware has caused trouble before, including clogged thrusters and a faulty computer, and earlier this year engineers replaced three devices on the probe with lower-power alternatives.

The mission began in 1977, when both Voyagers were launched to take advantage of a rare line-up of the planets. Voyager 1 passed Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980, photographed Earth as the “Pale Blue Dot” in 1990 and in 2012 became the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space, beyond the heliosphere, the bubble of particles and magnetic fields made by the Sun. It moves at about 38,000 mph (61,155 kph).

How much longer it can go on depends on power. Its generator turns heat from decaying plutonium into electricity, and both probes lose about 4 watts a year; NASA expects them to keep their current science instruments running until at least their 50th launch anniversaries next summer. Voyager 2 should reach the one-light-day mark in 2035.

did_you_know.text: The Peace Palace in The Hague, where the International Court of Justice sits, was built with money from the Scottish-American businessman Andrew Carnegie and opened in 1913.

explainer.title: The World Court and the Genocide Convention
body: The International Court of Justice was created in 1945 by the UN Charter as the United Nations’ main judicial body, and it sits in The Hague, in the Netherlands. It settles legal disputes between states; it does not put individual people on trial, which is the work of a separate body, the International Criminal Court.

The Genocide Convention was adopted by the UN General Assembly on 9 December 1948. It defines genocide as acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, and it obliges the states that join it to prevent and punish genocide. States that have joined can take disputes about the Convention to the ICJ, which is how The Gambia could bring its case against Myanmar. The court’s judgments are binding, but it has no police force: under Article 94 of the UN Charter, if a state ignores a judgment, the other side may turn to the UN Security Council.

lead.headline: A World Court Rules Against Myanmar
body: The International Court of Justice is the United Nations’ top court. On 19 November its judges ruled that Myanmar is responsible for genocide. Genocide means trying to destroy a whole group of people.
The group is the Rohingya, a Muslim minority. In 2017 Myanmar’s army carried out a crackdown. The court said about 10,000 Rohingya were killed. About 700,000 fled to Bangladesh.

The case was brought by The Gambia, a small country in West Africa. The judges voted 9 to 6. The court told Myanmar to pay compensation. It must also let Rohingya go home safely, if they choose to. Today about 1.2 million live in camps in Bangladesh.

world.headline: Europe Says ‘No New Yalta’
body: On 19 November the leaders of the US, Russia and China met in Shenzhen, China. Their statement did not mention the war in Ukraine.
European leaders worried. They remembered Yalta, a meeting in 1945. There, big powers shaped Europe after the Second World War. Smaller countries had little say.

Germany’s leader, Friedrich Merz, said Europe was divided up at Yalta. He said Europe would not let that happen again. Russia’s Putin said Yalta was not necessarily bad. He invited European leaders to Moscow for talks.

india.headline: India Makes a Bird Flu Vaccine for Chickens
body: Bird flu can kill almost all the chickens on a farm. To stop it spreading, farms have often had to kill whole flocks.
On 20 November India launched its own vaccine against the H5N1 bird flu virus. Scientists in Bhopal made it. It took three years.

The vaccine uses virus bits that have been made harmless. They cannot multiply. But they teach the chicken’s body to fight the real virus. Each dose may cost just Rs 1 to Rs 2. It could help more than 90 lakh poultry farmers.

politics_and_civics.headline: Congress Wins Many Village Council Seats in Rajasthan
body: Villages and districts in India elect local councils. These councils run local services. This system is called Panchayati Raj.
Rajasthan counted votes for its block and district councils on 20 November. Congress won 3,701 block seats. The BJP won 2,181.
This is surprising because the BJP runs Rajasthan’s state government. A Congress leader said villagers were unhappy with the government. A BJP spokesperson said the party would study what went wrong.

economics.headline: US Share Prices Fall Sharply
body: A share is a small piece of a company. On 20 November share prices in the US fell a lot. A big index called the S&P 500 was about 10% below its record.
Shares in artificial intelligence companies fell the most. Experts were worried about AI spending. They also expected interest rates to rise.
Markets in Japan and South Korea fell too. India’s market went up. The fall matters to families, because many retirement savings are kept in shares.

science_and_technology.headline: Voyager 1 Is One Light-Day Away
body: Voyager 1 is a NASA space probe. It was launched in 1977. On 18 November it reached one light-day from Earth. That is how far light travels in 24 hours.
No human-made object has gone farther. A message from Earth now takes a whole day to reach it. The answer takes another day to come back.
Voyager 1 has not sent science data since 14 November. But it still sends a simple signal, so engineers know where it is.
